n: Jesus keeps moving from town to town with a traveling missionary company. The good news (“glad tidings”) is that God’s kingdom has drawn near in Him, and the Twelve are learning by being at His side.

f.g: The Greek word behind this is the root of “evangel” or “gospel” — good news.

n: Luke alone names the women who traveled with Jesus. Many had been healed by Him, and their gratitude turned into discipleship. Mary Magdalene, freed from seven devils, later becomes the first witness of the risen Lord.

f.g: From Magdala, a fishing town on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

n: These women used their own money and goods to support Jesus and the Twelve. Joanna came from Herod Antipas’s own household, showing the gospel reaching even into the palace of the ruler of Galilee.

f.g: A manager of a household or estate — Chuza ran Herod’s affairs.
Out of their own possessions and means.

n: A huge crowd gathers from many towns, and Jesus teaches them with a parable — a short story from everyday life that carries a deeper spiritual lesson for those willing to seek it.

f.g: Greek parabolē, “a placing side by side” — a comparison that teaches by likeness.

n: Farmers in Galilee scattered seed by hand, so some landed on the hard footpaths between fields. Trampled by travelers and eaten by birds, it never had a chance to grow.

f.w: A sower went out to sow his seed

f.g: Birds.

n: Some seed fell where a thin layer of soil covered rock. It sprouted quickly, but with no depth to hold water its roots dried up and the plant died.

f.g: Matthew and Mark say it “had no root” and “no deepness of earth.”

n: Other seed landed in ground already full of thorn roots. Both grew together, but the thorns crowded out the grain and smothered it.

f.g: Strangled — deprived of light and space to grow.

n: Good soil produced a bumper harvest, a hundred times what was planted. Jesus then calls out a challenge: truly listen, and let the message sink in.

f.w: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear

f.g: A hundred times as much — an extraordinary, almost miraculous yield.

n: The disciples don’t pretend to understand. They ask. Their humble question opens the way for Jesus to explain, a pattern for anyone who studies the scriptures.
Parables both reveal and conceal. Those who seek receive the deeper meaning; those who don’t care hear only a story. God gives light as people are ready to receive it.

f.g: In the New Testament, truths that can only be known by revelation, not secrets kept from the faithful.

n: Jesus gives the key to the parable: the seed is God’s word. The story is really about different kinds of hearts and how they receive that word.

f.w: The seed is the word of God

n: The hard pathway is a heart that hears but never lets the word in. Before it can take root, the devil snatches it away so that it never leads to faith.

f.g: Greek diabolos, “accuser” or “slanderer.”

n: Rocky ground describes people who receive the gospel with excitement but never put down roots. When trials come, their shallow faith withers.

f.g: Here mainly testing or trial — pressures that reveal what a person’s faith is made of.

n: The thorny ground is a crowded life. Worries, wealth, and pleasures aren’t always evil in themselves, but they can slowly squeeze out spiritual growth until nothing ripens.

f.g: Their fruit never fully ripens — growth starts but never matures.

n: Good soil is an honest heart that hears, holds on, and keeps going. The fruit comes with patience — steady endurance over time, not instant results.

f.g: Greek kalos and agathos — noble and good; a sincere, well-prepared heart.

n: A lamp is meant to be seen. The light Jesus gives His disciples isn’t meant to be hidden but shared, so that others coming in can see too.

f.g: Really a small clay oil lamp, the common light source of the time.
A lampstand that held the lamp up so it lit the whole room.

n: Truth will not stay hidden forever. What God is teaching quietly now will one day be openly known, and every hidden thing will finally come to light.
How we listen matters. Those who use the light they receive are given more; those who neglect it lose even what they thought they had.

f.w: whosoever hath, to him shall be given

n: Mary and Jesus’ brothers come to see Him, but the crowd is so thick they cannot reach Him.

f.g: The crowd pressing in on every side.

n: Someone passes word through the crowd that His family is waiting outside.

f.g: Outside.

n: Jesus does not reject His family; He widens it. Everyone who hears God’s word and lives it becomes part of His true family.

f.w: hear the word of God, and do it

n: Jesus and His disciples set out by boat to cross the Sea of Galilee, a freshwater lake about 13 miles long.

f.g: Luke, who wrote for a Greek audience, calls it a lake rather than a sea — the Sea of Galilee.

n: Worn out, Jesus falls asleep. The lake sits low among hills, and sudden violent winds can sweep down onto it. Waves fill the boat and the crew is in real danger.

f.g: Danger.

n: The terrified disciples wake Him. With a word He rebukes the wind and waves, and the storm stops at once — a calm as sudden as the storm itself.
Jesus gently asks where their faith went. Their fear shifts from the storm to awe at Him: who can command nature itself? The answer is that the Creator is in the boat.

f.w: What manner of man is this!

n: They land on the eastern shore, opposite Galilee, in largely Gentile territory known as the Decapolis.

f.g: Ancient manuscripts vary (Gadarenes, Gerasenes, Gergesenes); all refer to the region southeast of the lake.

n: A man possessed for a long time meets them. He lives naked among the tombs, cut off from home and society — a picture of how completely evil can isolate and degrade a person.

f.g: Burial caves in hillsides; places Jews considered ritually unclean.

n: The evil spirits recognize Jesus immediately and name Him as the Son of the Most High God. They know who He is, and they fear His power.

f.w: What have I to do with thee
f.g: An idiom meaning “What do we have in common?” or “Leave me alone.”

n: Luke explains the backstory: Jesus had already ordered the spirit out. The man had been chained repeatedly, but he broke every restraint and was driven into the wilderness.

f.g: Shackles for the feet.

n: When Jesus asks his name, the answer is “Legion,” because so many devils had entered him.

f.g: A Roman army unit of several thousand soldiers — here meaning a vast number.

n: The spirits beg not to be sent into “the deep,” showing that even devils must submit to Christ’s authority.

f.g: Greek abyssos, the abyss — a place of confinement for evil spirits.

n: A large herd of pigs is grazing nearby — likely owned by Gentiles, since Jews considered swine unclean. The devils ask to enter them, and Jesus allows it.

f.g: Allowed.

n: The devils leave the man and enter the herd, which rushes down a steep slope into the lake and drowns. Their destructive nature is laid bare.

f.g: Drowned.

n: The herdsmen flee and spread the news through the town and countryside.

f.g: The herdsmen who tended the pigs.

n: People come and find the once-wild man sitting calmly at Jesus’ feet, dressed and sane. Yet instead of rejoicing, they are afraid.

f.w: sitting at the feet of Jesus
f.g: The posture of a disciple learning from a teacher.

n: Eyewitnesses explain how the possessed man was healed.

f.g: Controlled by evil spirits.

n: Overwhelmed with fear — and perhaps worried about their loss of property — the people ask Jesus to leave. He respects their choice and goes.

f.g: Begged Him to leave.

n: The healed man wants to stay with Jesus, but Jesus has a different mission for him.

f.g: Begged Him.

n: Jesus sends him home as a witness to his own people. Notice: Jesus says “God” did this, and the man tells what “Jesus” did — the two are united in the work.

f.g: Proclaimed openly.

n: Back on the Galilean side, a crowd is eagerly waiting for Jesus — a sharp contrast to the people who asked Him to leave.

f.g: Welcomed Him.

n: Jairus, a respected synagogue leader, sets aside his status and falls at Jesus’ feet, pleading for Him to come to his home.

f.g: A lay leader who arranged worship services in the local synagogue.

n: His only daughter, about twelve, is dying. As Jesus goes with him, the crowd presses in so closely He can barely move.

f.g: Was dying.
Crowded around and pressed against.

n: A woman has suffered bleeding for twelve years — as long as Jairus’s daughter has been alive. She has spent everything on doctors with no cure.

f.g: A chronic hemorrhage; under the law of Moses it also made her ritually unclean and isolated her socially.

n: She quietly touches the edge of His robe from behind, and the bleeding stops instantly.

f.g: Likely the tassels (fringes) Jewish men wore on the corners of their cloaks.
Stopped flowing.

n: Jesus asks who touched Him. Peter points out the obvious — everyone is bumping into Him! But Jesus means a different kind of touch: one of faith.

f.g: Greek epistatēs, “chief” or “commander” — a title of respect used only by Luke.

n: Jesus felt power go out of Him. Healing was not effortless or impersonal; He knew that a specific person had reached out in faith.

f.g: Power (Greek dynamis), not moral goodness.

n: Realizing she can’t remain hidden, the woman comes forward trembling and tells everyone what happened. Her healing becomes a public testimony.

f.w: declared unto him before all the people
f.g: Her public witness also restored her standing in the community.

n: Jesus calls her “Daughter” — a word of tenderness and belonging. He affirms her faith and sends her off in peace, healed in body and restored in spirit.

f.g: Greek sōzō, which can mean both “heal” and “save.”

n: While Jesus is still speaking, terrible news arrives: the girl has died. Don’t bother the Teacher anymore, the messenger says.

f.g: Here Greek didaskalos, “Teacher.”

n: Jesus immediately reassures Jairus: don’t be afraid, just keep believing. The delay that cost him precious time has not cost him his daughter.
Jesus takes only Peter, James, and John — the same three who later witness the Transfiguration and Gethsemane — along with the parents.
The house is full of mourners. Jesus says she is only sleeping — death, in His hands, is as temporary as sleep.

f.g: Mourned loudly; professional mourners were common at Jewish funerals.

f.w: she is not dead, but sleepeth

n: The mourners mock Him, certain she is dead. Their scorn sets up the miracle that follows.

f.g: Ridiculed Him.

n: Jesus clears the room, takes the girl’s hand, and simply tells her to get up.

f.g: Mark preserves His Aramaic words: “Talitha cumi.”

n: Her spirit returns to her body and she rises immediately. Jesus’ practical instruction to feed her shows His care for ordinary needs, and proves she is truly alive.

f.g: Death is the separation of spirit and body; here the spirit returns.
Food of any kind.

n: The parents are stunned. Jesus asks them to keep it quiet — perhaps to avoid crowds seeking only spectacle, since His time to be openly proclaimed had not yet come.

f.g: Instructed them firmly.
